name: Bank statement import
description: Use “Bank statement import” in Recued to bring a statement you exported yourself — CSV from any bank — into your own warehouse, with no aggregator in the middle. Aggregators gate real account data behind an approved business account; a file needs no credentials and no third party sees your transactions. You name your bank's columns once, so nothing is guessed. Re-importing an overlapping export skips lines you already have instead of double-counting them. Feeds ledger-book and expense-ledger.

operations.description: Record one statement line. Money is stored the way your export states it and not reinterpreted: a bank that prints ONE signed column fills `amount` (negative is money leaving), and a bank that prints a pair fills `money_in` and `money_out`. Recued does not fold a pair into a signed figure — which column means money out is a fact about your bank, not about statements, and a store that guessed it would hold a number no line of your file ever contained. Reading recipes combine the two; the stored line stays checkable against the paper.

Import a whole statement CSV in one gated call: you name your bank's columns, and every line is parsed, identified and recorded inside the warehouse. ONE approval covers the file — approving it once is the point, because approving a thousand rows one at a time is not review, it is clicking. Each column you name is stored verbatim in the field you name; nothing is combined or recalculated on the way in, so every stored line can be checked against the paper it came from. Re-importing an overlapping export adds only what is genuinely new: each line's id is derived from its own content and your account label, so the same line reproduces the same id rather than a second row. The result reports what landed AND what did not — rows written, rows you already had, rows refused, and any cell that would not parse, with its line number. An unreadable number is recorded as empty, never as zero: a zero looks like a real transaction for nothing, and that is how an import quietly reports the wrong balance. Set “Check first” to rehearse instead: every line is parsed and put through the same checks against your real data, then thrown away, so you can see what a run would do before anything is recorded. Worth doing the first time you map a new bank, because a column pointed at the wrong field imports perfectly well and is wrong in a way nothing can flag. ⚠ There are two ways to hand the file over and they are not interchangeable. `csv` is the text itself — that is the route for a file you picked from your own inventory, which is read first and passed in as text, exactly as before. `csv_ref` takes a file another step in the SAME run just produced (a converted spreadsheet, a filtered extract) and moves its contents straight into the warehouse without them passing through the recipe. You cannot choose, type or otherwise name a `csv_ref` — it only ever comes from a preceding step's output and stops existing when the run ends. Pass one or the other, never both.
Read one statement line by row id.

Page statement lines, most recently imported first. Filter on account_label, posted_on, currency, source_file, category. ⚠ Ordering is by when Recued recorded the line, NOT by the date printed on it: your bank's date is stored exactly as it wrote it (`20-Aug-2020`), and sorting text like that puts December before August. Reading a date would mean guessing your bank's format, and a guess about dates is how a statement silently reorders itself. Filter by `posted_on` to pick a day; the order within a page is the order the file listed. ⚠ Also not the importer's dedup path — a line's identity is its row id, derived from its own content, so `line.import` never reads anything back.
Change one statement line's owner-set fields under a CAS check — categorise it, name the counterparty, correct a mis-parsed amount.

Delete one statement line. Destructive: a deleted line is gone from every balance that summed it, and its row id goes with it — so a later re-import of the same export brings the line back rather than skipping it, because nothing is left to recognise it by.
